newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel drafts bill to reform, cut taxes in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Waigel drafts bill to reform, cut taxes in 1998.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Tuesday presented a draft tax reform bill that would bring forward 14 billion marks in planned tax cuts to 1998.
The bill, presented to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet, is part of a comprehensive two-stage tax reform plan agreed by coalition leaders to cut a total of 30 billion marks in taxes by 1999.
The tax reform is aimed at simplifying the system, stimulating corporate investment and creating jobs.
Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) have called for tax reforms to be implemented in full next year, but last week called the partial acceleration a step in the right direction.
Kohl is due to discuss the tax reform with SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine next Monday.
Waigel's bill includes a two percentage point reduction in the unpopular solidarity surcharge on income taxes, and would also cut corporate tax rates.

But it would also eliminate seven billion marks in tax benefits for corporations, particularly for additions to reserves. The government would have to fund about six billion marks in tax cuts through parallel reductions in spending.

Government spokesman Peter Hausmann said he hoped parliament would approve the bill before its summer break. A draft bill for the remainder of the planned tax reform will be ready next month, he said.
The government will talk with the SPD about bringing further pieces of the 1999 package ahead one year, if financing can be secured, Hausmann said.

The tax reform plan reached by a Waigel-led commission in January called for corporate taxes to be cut next year to 40 percent from 45 percent, and taxes on dividends to be cut to 28 percent from 30 percent.
The plan would reduce state government revenues by 1.3 billion marks and local government revenues by 168 million marks next year, but it would raise income in years following.
Joachim Poss, the SPD's parliamentary fiscal policy spokesman, said the delays in increased state and local revenues rendered the Waigel plan irresponsible.
